extracted.intended_audience: film enthusiasts, students of film criticism, and aspiring critics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted evaluative principles and standards Roger Ebert used in reviewing films: his genre-relative approach, technical and stylistic preferences, and scoring conventions, with examples and explanatory notes from the biography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black-and-white as a legitimate artistic choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Black-and-white is a legitimate and beautiful artistic choice in motion pictures, creating feelings and effects that cannot be obtained any other way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ebert argued black-and-white (or 'silver-and-white') 'creates a mysterious dream state, a simpler world of form and gesture.' He gives a practical test (shooting natural-light closeups in black-and-white to see an 'aura of mystery') as evidence that B&W can produce moods and effects unattainable with color. Anti-pattern: assuming B&W is merely 'missing something' compared with color.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value animation for expressing essence and wonder
rubrics_metrics.description: Animation is freed from gravity and the chains of the possible; it 'shows [a film's] essence' and creates a new existence in its own right rather than being a copy of 'real movies.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ebert champions animation (e.g., Miyazaki) because it can present 'wondrous sights not available in the real world' and set myth and dreams free. He rejects the notion that animation is 'just for children' and emphasizes its capacity to create unique cinematic experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: A great documentary can be about anything if seen well
rubrics_metrics.description: They say you can make a great documentary about anything, as long as you see it well enough and truly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ebert uses Gates of Heaven (about pet cemeteries) to show how a documentary can grow from a narrow subject to address 'love, immortality, failure, and the dogged elusiveness of the American Dream.' He treats good documentaries as potentially more absorbing and entertaining than fiction and stresses the importance of the filmmaker's perception and presentation. Anti-pattern: dismissing documentaries because of subject matter alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate a movie by how good it is of its type (genre-relative assessment)
rubrics_metrics.description: I've always preferred a generic approach to film criticism; I ask myself how good a movie is of its type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ebert assesses films relative to genre expectations and aims — e.g., crediting horror directors who genuinely frighten audiences, or judging children's movies by whether they provide imagination and inventiveness appropriate to that audience. This implies that excellence is context-dependent: a film should be judged on how well it achieves the goals of its genre rather than by a single universal standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Children's films should not be graded on a curve
rubrics_metrics.description: Ebert did not believe in grading children's movies on a curve, as he thought children were smarter than given credit for and deserved quality entertainment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He argues that kids are 'among the sharpest' and that children's films should offer life, imagination, fantasy, inventiveness — not just 'not have anything bad in them.' Anti-pattern: excusing shoddy or witless work because the intended audience is children.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not judge a film primarily by its ideology
rubrics_metrics.description: Ebert tried not to judge a film on its ideology; he believed films are superb for presenting moods and feelings rather than for dealing with abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using Apocalypse Now as example, he notes that films recreate experiences and moods rather than analyze abstract ideas; thus reviews should emphasize how a film presents a state of mind, atmosphere, or sensory experience rather than whether its explicit 'ideas' align with the critic's politics or beliefs. Anti-pattern: dismissing or praising a film mainly for agreement/disagreement with its stated ideology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit filmmakers who fully commit to their chosen effect (e.g., fear in thrillers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Credit must be paid to directors who want to really frighten us, to make a good thriller when quite possibly a bad one would have made as much money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ebert defends directors who aim for strong emotional effects (like genuine terror) even if some readers object to the content. The reviewer's role is to describe effectiveness within the chosen aim, not necessarily to 'support' every moral implication of the content. Anti-pattern: condemning a film solely because its aims make the reviewer uncomfortable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appreciate novelty — films that show you something new
rubrics_metrics.description: I'm grateful to movies that show me what I haven't seen before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ebert defends films (even 'goofy' ones) that offer novel sights or experiences (example: Speed 2's cruise-ship main-street sequence). Novelty and the capacity to present previously unseen images or imaginative set pieces are positive attributes, even if the film is otherwise criticized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical effects should aid storytelling, not distract (skepticism of 3D gimmickry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ebert was skeptical of the resurgence of 3D effects in film, which he found unrealistic and distracting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He prioritized visual realism and the integrity of cinematic presentation; effects that draw attention to themselves or reduce clarity of storytelling are negatives. Conversely, he advocated technical improvements that enhance the viewing experience (see frame rate and projection guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection and presentation quality matter (support for higher frame rates and proper projection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ebert was a strong advocate for Maxivision 48 (48 frames per second) and opposed theaters lowering projector bulb intensity to extend bulb life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He argued that exhibition practices that reduce visibility or alter the filmmaker's intended look (e.g., dimming bulbs) are detrimental; conversely, technical standards that improve clarity and fidelity (higher frame rates, correct projection brightness) are to be supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of star ratings: 3 out of 4 stars is a 'thumbs up' threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: Ebert acknowledged he gave higher ratings on average than other critics, noting that he considered a rating of 3 out of 4 stars to be the general threshold for a film to get a 'thumbs up.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using Ebert's star ratings, understand his scale context: 3/4 is positive; his average translated percentage (71%) was higher than some peers. This is explicit scoring guidance useful for interpreting his reviews comparatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider context and meaning when evaluating content and ratings (critique of MPAA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ebert's main arguments about the MPAA were that they were too strict on sex and profanity, too lenient on violence, secretive with their guidelines, inconsistent in applying them and not willing to consider the wider context and meaning of the film.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ebert believed content should be evaluated with attention to context, intent, and meaning rather than by rigid or secretive rules. He advocated more transparent, consistent, and context-sensitive classification practices and even supported rethinking rating categories (e.g., replacing NC-17 with separate ratings for pornographic and nonpornographic adult films). Anti-pattern: mechanical or context-blind application of content standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness in representation — characters need not serve as group emissaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Ebert defended the right of Asian-American characters (and by extension characters from any group) 'to be whoever the hell they want to be' and argued they do not have to represent 'their people.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating portrayals of race or identity, critics should resist the expectation that every character must serve as a representative or moral exemplar of their group. Critique should focus on the work's artistic and narrative qualities and avoid condescending standards that require minority characters to 'represent' their people in a particular way.
